title: The senses walk out
hookLine: the senses quarrel over which of them matters most, and they settle it by leaving the body one at a time
carry: prana: the breath that holds the rest
last: OM: OM: THE ESSENCE OF ESSENCES OF ESSENCES.

cards: Sooner or later, every team has this argument. The one who talks to the clients says the company runs on them. The one who builds the product says nothing exists without them.
The planner says without a plan it's all chaos.
The Chandogya Upanishad tells the same fight, only the team is inside your own body: speech, the eye, the ear, the mind and the breath, arguing over which of them is the greatest.
The way they settle it is brilliant, and a little brutal.

teach.b: They go to Prajapati, the lord of creatures, and ask him to judge. His test: the greatest is the one whose leaving makes the body worst off. So they take turns walking out.
Speech leaves for a whole year. Back again, it asks how they managed. Like someone who can't speak, the others say.
We breathed, we saw, we heard, we thought. We got by. The eye leaves for a year, and they get by like someone who can't see.
The ear leaves, and they live like someone who can't hear. The mind leaves, and they live, the text says, like small children whose minds haven't grown yet. Each time, the body carries on.

Then breath gets ready to go. And here's the picture that makes the story stick: as a strong horse, pulling away, tears up the pegs it was tethered to, the breath begins to tear up all the others with it.

teach.h: SPEECH, EYE, EAR, MIND: THE BODY GETS BY.
teach.b: Speech, eye, ear and mind come running.

teach.h: THE HORSE TEARS UP ITS PEGS.
teach.b: Stay, they say. You're the greatest of us. That full story sits in chapter five of the Chandogya.
Chapter one has a shorter one: gods and demons fight, and the demons spoil speech, eye, ear and mind with evil.
But when they strike the breath in the mouth, the chief breath, they shatter like a clod of earth thrown at a rock. In both places, breath holds the rest.
And chapter five ends by saying people don't call the senses speech, eyes, ears and minds.
They call them all pranas, breaths.
That's why breath is treated as sacred: many Hindus begin worship with pranayama, tending the breath, and when a temple image is consecrated, the rite is prana pratishtha, setting the breath in.

how: Many Hindus practice pranayama, the regulation of breath, before worship and in yoga; when an image is installed in a temple or home shrine, the rite of prana pratishtha 'sets the breath' in it.

o: an inner voice that speaks before words come out
life-breath, the one that holds all the other senses
a stretching pose held in yoga to calm the body

games.q: who left, and how the body got by — tap the pairs.

s: in the story, the body dies when speech leaves
speech is gone a whole year, and the body gets by, like someone who can't speak.
the text compares breath to a horse tearing up its tethering pegs
as breath starts to go, it pulls the other senses up with it.
the text says the senses are all called pranas, breaths
breath holds the rest, so the Chandogya says people name them all after it. it's why the consecration rite is called prana pratishtha.

games.q: you're Prajapati. the senses want you to say which of them is greatest. how do you judge?
o: let each one leave the body for a while, and see whose absence hurts most.
say they're all equal and send them home.
games.why: the test is absence. speech, eye, ear and mind each leave for a year and the body manages. when breath starts to go, everything comes with it.

practice: Give the senses the day off: let your eyes close, let the room's sounds fall to the background, stay silent, and let thoughts drift past without chasing them.
Then notice what's still going without being asked, in and out, the one the others ran back to. Just keep it company.

wordCard.voice: Prana, life-breath. When breath prepares to leave the body, like a strong horse tearing up its tethering pegs, speech, eye, ear and mind come running, calling it the greatest of them all.

orig.note: Sanskrit prāṇa: breath, life-breath. the Chandogya says the senses are all called prāṇas, after their chief.

carryVoice: Your line: prana, the breath that holds the rest. The others can step out for a year; breath can't. Day three hundred thirty-three, done.
